item.title: 2nd place on TinyLaunch
item.description: The TinyLaunch campaign is over: FlowGroove finished 2nd. What two weeks of launching taught a solo dev, and what happens now.
item.content:encoded:
## The result
The TinyLaunch run is over, and **FlowGroove finished in 2nd place**. There's a silver badge in the footer now.
A week ago this app launched into a batch of polished marketing and AI tools — a metronome-and-setlist app for cover bands, built by one person. It spent launch day at #1 and held near the top until the end. Second overall is more than I planned for, and I'll take it with both hands.
## What the launch actually gave me
Not the badge. The launch forced a week of honesty: real users on real phones, finding real problems. iPhone sign-in that broke in three different ways until it didn't. Avatars that vanished on desktop. A support link that led nowhere on some networks. All of it found because strangers clicked a link, and all of it fixed because they told me.
That's what a launch is for, I think. The leaderboard is the excuse; the users are the prize.
## What happens now
The app has a proper home at [app.flowgroove.app](https://app.flowgroove.app) — faster deploys, cleaner sign-in, same free everything. The devlog keeps going, one story a day, because the backlog of things bands need is not getting shorter.
If you voted: thank you. If you're in a band and haven't tried it yet — [the demo is real](https://flowgroove.app): three bands, real songs, real setlists, no sign-up. Second place on a launch board, but for the next rehearsal your band runs with it, it only has to be first choice once.

item.title: #1 on launch day
item.description: FlowGroove is sitting at #1 on TinyLaunch right now. A thank-you, and an honest note on what a leaderboard number does and doesn’t mean.
item.content:encoded:
## What happened
As I write this, **FlowGroove is #1 on TinyLaunch** — 39 upvotes, ahead of a couple of sharp marketing and AI tools. A metronome-and-setlist app for cover bands, at the top of a launch board. I did not have that on the card.
Thank you. Genuinely. Every one of those votes is a person who read one line — *keep your band in sync: setlists, tempo, concert mode* — and decided that was worth a click. That's not nothing.
## The honest part
A leaderboard is a vanity number. It measures a good day, not a good product. The number I actually watch is smaller and quieter: a band opening a setlist five minutes before they go on, the metronome not drifting, the sync holding on bad venue wifi. That's the win that doesn't show up on a launch board.
So I'm keeping this in proportion — grateful for the day, back to the work tomorrow. If the line above sounds like your band, [try it](https://flowgroove.app). It's free, and the demo account is real: three bands, real songs, real setlists, no sign-up.
To everyone who voted, and to the bands already using it on stage — thank you. This is a better week because of you.

item.title: Getting FlowGroove ready for TinyLaunch
item.description: After months of building and three gigs run entirely on the app, I’m taking FlowGroove public with a TinyLaunch campaign.
item.content:encoded:
For months FlowGroove has been a quiet project — built between rehearsals, tested at my own gigs. Three shows now, run entirely on the app: songs, setlists, the metronome, all of it on stage with me instead of a folder of coffee-stained paper.
Along the way I fixed a long list of small annoyances and a few genuinely scary bugs. Somewhere in there it stopped feeling like a prototype and started feeling like something I trust in front of an audience.
So it's time to say the word out loud. I'm starting a TinyLaunch campaign for FlowGroove — not to chase numbers, but to find the people who'd actually use it: bands drowning in the same scattered-chat, lost-setlist, "what's the BPM again?" chaos I built this to fix. I want testers, honest feedback, and a few more musicians I can help untangle their band's mess.
If that's you — or you know a band like that — cheer me and FlowGroove on. This is the part where it stops being just mine.

item.title: In-app help that follows the screen you're on
item.description: Per-screen help pages now live inside FlowGroove — open the wiki panel and you get docs for exactly the screen you’re looking at, not a generic manual.
item.content:encoded:
## What changed
FlowGroove now has built-in help that's aware of where you are. The same Markdown pages that power the docs site are bundled into the app, and on desktop a wiki panel opens beside what you're doing and shows the page for that exact screen.
- Help docs are written once as Hugo Markdown and reused — site and app read the same source, so they can't drift apart. - On desktop the builder splits into two columns: your work on the right, the relevant help page rendered on the left, with overlays kept out of your way. - Front-matter is stripped and each screen maps to its own page, so opening help from the metronome gives you metronome docs, not a table of contents to dig through.
## Why it matters
The thing I always hated in band apps: you're mid-rehearsal, you tap "help," and you land on a generic FAQ that has nothing to do with the button you were poking at. Now the help knows the screen. Less hunting, more playing.

item.title: 5 Problems Every Cover Band Faces (And How I Fixed Them)
item.description: The 5 most common problems every cover band faces during rehearsals and gigs, and how FlowGroove solves each one.
item.content:encoded:
# 5 Problems Every Cover Band Faces (And How I Fixed Them)
Ten years of cover bands, and somehow every single one of them ran into the same five problems. So I'll walk you through them — and how FlowGroove deals with each.
---
## Problem #1: The lost setlist
You show up to rehearsal and the setlist — the one piece of paper — is gone. Coffee got on it, or it's at home, or someone "forgot." Now you're spending the first fifteen minutes going "wait, what were we playing?"
FlowGroove keeps your setlists digital and synced across every device. No paper, no coffee casualties, no excuses. Add songs in a few seconds, share with the band, done.
---
## Problem #2: The BPM argument
"Is 'Wonderwall' 87 or 89?" "Does it matter?" It matters when the drummer counts in at 95 and the whole thing wobbles off a cliff. Then it's five minutes of tapping tempo and checking YouTube while the energy drains out of the room.
FlowGroove pulls the BPM for you — type the song name and there it is. If the lookup is ever down, you can enter it by hand. Nothing blocks you.
---
## Problem #3: The key-change confusion
"What key is this?" "I thought G." "No, F#m." *plays a chord* "...yeah, that's not it." Ten minutes of transposition and capo math later, you've lost the thread.
FlowGroove detects the key the same way: type the song, get the key. The guitarist works out the capo, the keys player preps the chords, and everyone's finally on the same page.
---
## Problem #4: The device disconnect
You updated the setlist on your phone. The guitarist has last week's version on his tablet. The drummer printed it out in 2023. Three people, three different setlists, zero agreement.
FlowGroove syncs in real time. Change a song on your phone and it updates on everyone's screen almost immediately — even on patchy venue internet. One setlist, everywhere.
---
## Problem #5: The dark gig
You're on stage, it's dim, you pull out your phone to check what's next, and the screen lights up the whole front row — right into the bass player's eyes.
FlowGroove has a proper stage-ready dark mode: high-contrast, easy to read, and it won't blind your bandmates. Built for dark venues and late nights.
---
## The common thread
Every one of these comes down to the same thing: the right tool just didn't exist for us.
- Paper setlists → digital ones - BPM arguments → automatic detection - Key confusion → key detection - Mismatched devices → real-time sync - Blinding screens → dark mode
That's the whole reason FlowGroove exists. Not because I could build it — because I was tired of not having it.
## What FlowGroove does
It's a free, real-time setlist sync app for cover bands. It handles all five problems above, plus a couple you haven't hit yet:
- Auto BPM & key detection for any song - Real-time setlist sync across every device - Offline mode for signal-free rehearsal rooms - Stage-ready dark mode for gigs - Free for indie musicians
No corporate team, no venture capital — just a musician who got tired of the chaos.
## Try it
[Try the FlowGroove demo](https://app.flowgroove.app/) — no registration needed.
If it helps your band, you can [support development on Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/flowgroove). Every donation keeps the servers running and the coffee flowing.
---
**What does YOUR band struggle with? [Tell me](mailto:hello@flowgroove.app) — I might build the fix.** 🎸
*Got a feature in mind? [Open an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/berlogabob/flutter-FlowGroove-app/issues).*

item.title: Why I Built FlowGroove Between Rehearsals
item.description: The story of how 10 years in cover bands led me to build FlowGroove as a solo developer, one late night at a time.
item.content:encoded:
# Why I Built FlowGroove Between Rehearsals
I've played in cover bands for about ten years, and I write software for a living. For the longest time those two lives never touched — until one of them got annoying enough to fix with the other.
## The problem that wouldn't go away
You know the drill:
- Paper setlists that got coffee-stained or lost - Nobody remembering the BPM for "Wonderwall" - The eternal "was it F#m or Gm?" debate - Five minutes lost between songs while we found the right version - My phone, the guitarist's tablet, and the drummer's laptop all showing something different
We spent more time organizing than playing. And the tools that were supposed to help? Either too complicated to set up, too expensive for a hobby, or buggy enough to crash mid-rehearsal. Cool.
## The breaking point
One Tuesday night, our third rehearsal in a row got derailed because someone lost the setlist. Again. And it hit me: I do this for a living. I build things. Why was I putting up with this?
So I stopped putting up with it.
## Building it
FlowGroove got built the way side projects always do — late nights, weekends, and a lot of coffee. My rules for it were simple:
- **A song should take seconds to add.** Slower than that and the band won't bother. - **BPM and key should fill themselves in.** Manual entry is where good intentions go to die. - **It has to sync in real time.** I change it, everyone sees it. - **It has to work offline.** Rehearsal rooms eat WiFi for breakfast. - **Dark mode.** Nobody wants a flashlight on stage. - **Free for indie musicians.** Because we are not a wealthy people.
## The tech, briefly
I went with **Flutter** — one codebase for web, iOS, and Android, fast to iterate on, and decent-looking without much fighting. **Firebase Firestore** does the heavy lifting on sync: change something and it shows up on everyone else's screen almost immediately, even on a wobbly venue connection.
## What I learned
Building a product alone is hard, and also kind of great.
On the technical side: real-time sync is sneakier than it looks, offline-first isn't optional for musicians, and "dark mode" is really about contrast, not just a black background.
On the not-technical side: "free" doesn't mean "worthless," it means the value shows up somewhere else. And people will support an honest solo project on Ko-fi if you're actually honest with them.
## Where it's at now
FlowGroove is live, it's free, and it does the job:
- Real-time sync across devices, fast enough to feel instant - Auto BPM and key — type the song, get the data - Full offline mode - A dark theme built for dim venues
## What's next
No dates, just the list: an iOS build, more metadata sources (Spotify, YouTube), transposition and capo helpers, and proper band collaboration with shared libraries and comments.
## Support the journey
If any of this rings true, or if FlowGroove ends up saving your band a few headaches, you can support it on Ko-fi.
[**Support the dev on Ko-fi**](https://ko-fi.com/flowgroove)
Every bit keeps the servers running and the coffee flowing.
---
**Thanks for reading. Now go make some music.** 🎸
*Questions? [Email me](mailto:hello@flowgroove.app) or [open an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/berlogabob/flutter-FlowGroove-app/issues).*

item.title: AI & Import
item.description:
AI & Import

Get songs in fast — bring your own AI, no in-app tokens.

Search to autofill

  • When adding a song, search by title. Suggestions come from your library, Spotify and MusicBrainz, ranked by relevance.
  • Pick a Spotify result to autofill BPM and key automatically.

Import & export

  • Import: paste CSV or FlowGroove Song JSON (the app detects which), see a preview of what will be added or merged, then save.
  • Export: a song as JSON (Copy as JSON), or a song/setlist as a printable PDF.

Use your own AI

  • In the Import dialog, tap Copy AI prompt.
  • Paste it into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini and let it write the song.
  • Copy the result and paste it back into Import.

Connect an AI agent (MCP)

Let Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini list and add songs in your library directly.

item.title: Bands
item.description:
Bands

Organize rehearsals with your group.

  • Create a band, then invite members with a join link.
  • Membership is managed on the server — joins go through a secure flow.
  • Each band has its own songs, setlists, and about page.
  • Band setlists export and share just like personal ones: the card’s ⋯ menu offers Copy links and Export PDF (As is / Compact), and the metronome button queues the whole setlist.
  • Plan the next session with Rehearsals — an availability poll that turns into a confirmed rehearsal with a setlist.

item.title: Concert Mode
item.description:
Concert Mode

Perform a setlist live.

  • Open a setlist to enter Concert Mode.
  • Swipe between songs; key details stay on screen.
  • Keep the metronome running between songs.
  • Tap the lyrics button to open the current song’s Performance sheet — its chords and lyrics, seeded with the live tempo, while the click keeps running.

item.title: Home
item.description:
Home

Your dashboard. From here you can jump to your songs, bands, setlists, and tools.

  • Tap a navigation tab at the bottom to switch sections.
  • Menu (⋯) in the bottom bar opens the current screen’s actions and your Profile.
  • The practice dashboard on top shows this week’s minutes, streak and a 7-day graph — tap it for the full Practice screen.
  • Quick Actions: create a Song, Band or Setlist — or Audio note, which starts recording the moment it opens (link it to a song later from the Recorder).
  • Tools: Tuner, Metronome, Rehearsals, Recorder (all your unlinked takes in one place) and Practice on the full-width bottom row.

item.title: Metronome
item.description:
Metronome

Practice to a steady beat.

  • Set the tempo (BPM) and time signature — the two dot rows are labeled Beats and Subdivision.
  • Tap accents to emphasize beats.
  • Menu (⋯) in the bottom bar holds Sound, Count-in, Ramp, Haptics and the save-to-song actions; toggles flip right inside the sheet.
  • Unloading the current song can be undone from the snackbar.
  • On the web, audio uses the Web Audio engine automatically.

item.title: Practice

Practice

Your practice, tracked automatically — every metronome session is logged (when it started, how long, which song, at what BPM). Nothing to set up.

item.title: Profile
item.description:
Profile

Your account. Open it from Menu (⋯) in the bottom bar. App-wide preferences live in Settings.

  • Update your display name and photo.
  • Set your music roles.
  • Link Telegram — get your name/photo and band notifications there.
  • Sign out from the button at the bottom of this screen.
  • Delete account (at the bottom) permanently removes your account and all your data.

item.title: Setlists
item.description:
Setlists

Order songs for a performance.

  • Create a setlist and add songs from your library or a band.
  • Tapping a setlist opens a read-only view first — editing is behind the explicit Edit action (in the Menu sheet), so nothing gets reordered by accident.
  • In the editor, long-press a song and drag to reorder it.
  • If a song was deleted from the library it still shows in the setlist as “Unavailable song” — the count stays honest and you decide when to remove the entry (swipe it away; Undo appears if you change your mind).
  • Deleting a setlist can also be undone from the snackbar for a few seconds.
  • Open a setlist in Concert Mode to perform.
  • Each setlist card shows one pinned quick-action button plus a ⋯ menu. Choose what the pinned button does in Settings → Quick action on setlist cards (default Open in metronome, which queues the whole setlist).
  • The ⋯ menu has: Edit setlist, Event kit, Share (songs as links), Copy links, and Export PDF — As is (one detailed card per song) or Compact (one line per song, fits a single list).

Event Kit — the show, not just the songs

Open Event kit from a setlist card’s ⋯ menu; a small 🎭 badge on the card shows once a kit is set up. For setlists tied to a real event:

item.title: Settings
item.description:
Settings

All app-wide preferences in one place. Open Menu (⋯) in the bottom bar — Settings sits right under your profile.

item.title: Songs
item.description:
Songs

Your personal song library.

  • Menu (⋯) in the bottom bar holds the library tools: Browse catalog, Find duplicates, Import from CSV, Export to CSV.

  • The Key / BPM filter understands flats and minors — filtering by G# also finds songs saved as Ab, and the Major/Minor toggle switches the key chips. BPM presets match the song’s exact Our BPM; songs without one stay visible.

  • The pinned button on each song card is your quick action — long-press the card’s ⋯ menu → Quick action… to choose what it does (Metronome, Tuner, Play on Spotify, …). The icon changes to match.

  • Tap a song to open its page — one home with three tabs: Sheet (play from it), Edit (details + song structure) and Lab (the song’s journal). The page’s ⋯ menu carries the song tools: Metronome, Open in Tuner, Play on Spotify, Add to band…, Export PDF, Export ChordPro.

  • Tap + to add a song (title, BPM, key, structure, links).

  • Search to autofill from the online catalog. Matches come from MusicBrainz (title, artist, album, release info). Type the artist as well as the title (e.g. light my fire the doors) to pull the right recording to the top — on a bare title there are often many same-named covers and the real one can’t be told apart. Selecting a match fills those fields in, and tempo/key are added from Deezer when available. Your own library is deliberately left out of these suggestions so you don’t match a song against itself.

  • Provenance links, added for you. When you accept a match, FlowGroove drops links into the song so you can see where the info came from and jump straight to the source — the MusicBrainz recording, the Spotify track (when known), plus YouTube, chords and lyrics searches. They show up as chips under Links; tap one to open it.

  • Lyrics + a song map, fetched. Plain lyric text is pulled in automatically and split into Verse / Chorus sections, so it shows up on the song’s Sheet ready to play from. Chords aren’t available from a free catalogue — paste a ChordPro chart (below) for the full chords.

  • Add lyrics + chords (ChordPro) per section in the Edit tab’s song structure. Import lyrics & chords takes a pasted full chart and fills title, key, tempo, time and the whole structure at once.

  • The Sheet tab is the performance sheet — it opens first when you tap a song, and Concert Mode’s lyrics button lands there too. It keeps the screen awake, lets you transpose live (the ± controls sit in the bottom bar), and auto-scrolls hands-free: press play and set the pace, or switch to BPM mode to scroll at a speed matched to the tempo. The Stage button goes full-screen for the gig.

  • Export from the song page’s ⋯ menu: a song sheet as PDF — either As is (full size, flows across pages) or Compact (everything scaled to fit one A4 page) — or as a standard ChordPro .cho file to share or print. The PDF header carries key, scale, tempo, time signature and the song map.

  • CSV export/import now carries the per-section chords too, so your chart survives a trip through a spreadsheet.

  • Song cards lead with the full-width title; below it a meta rail shows the key chip, tempo, and — for band copies — who added the song.

  • Songs you add to a band become independent copies in that band — editing the band’s copy changes only that copy, not your personal song.

item.title: Tuner
item.description:
Tuner

Tune your instrument by ear or display.

  • Play a note; the tuner shows the detected pitch.
  • The microphone button’s left companion is a live input-level meter — if it stays empty, the tuner isn’t hearing you.
  • Use Stage Mode for a large, glanceable display.
